title: How to Dispute a Credit Report Error: A Beginner's Guide
description: How to dispute a credit report error in the US: get your free reports, gather proof, file with the bureau and the lender, and what to do next.
keywords: how to dispute credit report error credit report dispute letter remove late payment credit freeze
takeaways: Disputing an error is free, and the bureaus must investigate, usually within 30 days.
Dispute with the bureau and with the company that reported it, and send copies of your proof.
If an account is not yours, freeze your credit at all the bureaus too.
body:
A mistake on your credit report is one of those problems that feels personal. A late payment you never missed, a balance you paid off, or a stranger's account can pull your score down and cost you money: a bigger deposit on an apartment, a worse loan rate, or a flat no from a lender. The fix is less scary than the problem. Disputing an error is free, it is your legal right in the US under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and the bureaus have to investigate when you ask. This guide covers the whole job: getting your reports, spotting what is wrong, writing the dispute, and what to do if the bureau says no. If an apartment application is coming up, [first apartment costs](/blog/first-apartment-costs/) shows why sorting this out early matters. ## Step 1: Get your free credit reports In the US, start at AnnualCreditReport.com, the one site federal law authorizes for free credit reports. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notes that the three bureaus have permanently extended free weekly reports through that site, on top of the free report each bureau owes you every 12 months. Pull all three reports: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Each bureau keeps its own file on you, and they do not share corrections, so an error can sit on one report and nowhere else. Save a copy of each report and note the date. You will need exact account names, numbers, and dates later. A dispute written from memory is one that gets rejected as too vague. New to all this? [How to build credit from scratch](/blog/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch/) explains what a report and a score actually are. ## Step 2: Read each report and mark what is wrong Read slowly, section by section, looking for anything that is wrong, incomplete, out of date, or not yours. These errors show up most often: | What to check | What an error looks like | |---------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Accounts | An account you never opened, or one belonging to a relative with a similar name | | Payment history | A late payment marked for a month you paid on time | | Balances and limits | A balance you already paid down, or a limit listed lower than your real one | | Duplicates | The same debt listed twice, sometimes under two different company names | | Account status | An account you closed shown as open, or a paid account still shown as unpaid | | Personal details | A misspelled name or an address you never lived at | One honest limit: a dispute is for information that is wrong. If you genuinely missed a payment, the bureau may keep reporting it. The FTC points out that most accurate negative information can stay on your report for seven years, and bankruptcy information for ten. ## Step 3: Gather your proof before you file Paper beats opinions. A dispute with nothing attached often ends with the bureau taking the lender's word over yours. For each error, find the document that proves it: a bank statement showing the payment, a receipt, a payoff letter, or a statement with the correct balance. Two rules both the CFPB and the FTC repeat: send copies, never originals, and keep a copy of everything. If an account is not yours and identity theft might be behind it, say so in your dispute and visit IdentityTheft.gov, the FTC's recovery site, because that problem needs more than a correction. ## Step 4: File the dispute, twice over First, dispute with every credit bureau that shows the error, online, by phone, or by mail. Mail is slower, but it creates a paper trail. The CFPB suggests certified mail with a return receipt requested, so you have proof of the day it arrived. The investigation clock runs from the day the bureau receives your dispute, so that proof is worth having. Second, dispute with the company that reported the information, known as the furnisher: the bank, card company, lender, or debt collector named on your report. The FTC explains that if the furnisher finds its information was wrong, it must notify all three nationwide bureaus so they can fix their files. That saves you chasing the same error three times. The FTC lists these mailing addresses for disputes: | Bureau | Mailing address for disputes | |------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------| | Equifax | Equifax Information Services LLC, P.O. Box 740256, Atlanta, GA 30348 | | Experian | Experian, P.O. Box 4500, Allen, TX 75013 | | TransUnion | TransUnion LLC Consumer Dispute Center, P.O. Box 2000, Chester, PA 19016 | ## A dispute letter you can copy and adapt Your letter needs no legal language. It needs specifics: what the report says, what is actually true, what proof you are enclosing, and what you want done. This one follows the CFPB and FTC sample letters. Replace anything in brackets with your own details. > [Your full name] > > [Your street address] > > [City, State, ZIP] > > [Date] > > [Bureau name and mailing address, from the table above] > > Dear Sir or Madam, > > I am writing to dispute information in my credit report, confirmation number [your confirmation number, if you have one]. > > Item disputed: [lender or company name], account number [account number as shown on your report]. My report shows [a 30-day late payment for January 2026]. This is incorrect. [I paid on time. My bank statement shows the $64 payment left my account on January 9, 2026, three days before the due date.] > > Please investigate this item and remove the incorrect late payment. Enclosed are a copy of the report page with the item circled, and a copy of my bank statement showing the payment. > > Please send me the results of your investigation in writing. > > Sincerely, > > [Your name] > > Enclosures: [list what you enclosed] Send one letter to each bureau that shows the error, plus a matching letter to the furnisher. Several errors can share one letter, as long as each item gets its own short paragraph like the one above. ## Worked example: one wrong late payment, start to finish An illustration with made-up details, so you can see how the pieces fit together: Say your Experian report, pulled on March 3, shows a 30-day late payment on your store card for January. You are sure you paid, and your bank statement backs you up: the $64 payment left your account on January 9, before the January 12 due date. - March 5: You mail your dispute letter to Experian by certified mail, enclosing the report page (late payment circled) and the bank statement. A shorter version goes to the store card company the same day. - March 6 to early April: Experian investigates, forwarding your dispute and documents to the card company, which checks its records against your statement. - April 2: The written results arrive, 28 days after you mailed the letter. The late payment is gone, and Experian includes a free updated copy of your report. You check Equifax and TransUnion and confirm the error never appeared there. Total cost: postage for two letters. Total time: about four weeks. What made it work was keeping copies of every page, the same habit behind [the 20-minute monthly money review](/blog/monthly-money-review/). ## What happens while you wait The FTC says the bureau has 30 days to investigate. That window can stretch to 45 days if you send extra evidence after the investigation has started. While it runs, the bureau forwards your dispute and documents to the furnisher, which has to investigate too. When the investigation ends, the bureau must send you the results in writing. If anything changed, you also get a free copy of your updated report, and it does not count as one of your free reports. You can also ask the bureau to send the correction to anyone who got your report in the past six months, or two years for employment checks. One trap to avoid: a bureau can refuse a dispute it reasonably decides is frivolous, such as one that never states what is being disputed. The CFPB notes the bureau then has to notify you within five business days and explain why. Specifics protect you: name the account, the date, and the exact wrong entry. Keeping a simple record of each dispute, with the date sent, the bureau, the deadline, and the result, makes the waiting easier. If you would rather not build that record from scratch, we put together a free tracker for exactly this job.

Download the free Credit Report Dispute Tracker (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The credit report dispute tracker with one sample dispute and the date a reply is expected](/assets/img/posts/credit-report-dispute-tracker-preview-1280x337.webp) ## If the bureau says the information is "verified" This is the reply nobody wants: the investigation ends, the error stays, and the letter says the information was verified. It happens, and it is not the end of the road. - Read the results letter closely. Sometimes "verified" only means the furnisher confirmed its own records, and its records are exactly what is wrong. - Dispute again, but bring new evidence. A second dispute that repeats the first one word for word can be brushed aside. One with a new document, such as a letter from the lender admitting the mistake, is a fresh claim. - If you have only disputed with one side so far, now dispute with the other: bureau or furnisher. - Ask the bureau to add a statement of dispute. The FTC explains that this statement, in your own words, is included in future reports, so reviewers can see you disagree. - Still stuck? In the US, file a complaint with the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov/complaint. Describe what happened, attach your letters and evidence, and state the outcome you want. Companies take these seriously, because a regulator is now reading the file. If an error is costing you a home, a job, or serious money and nothing moves, talk to a consumer law attorney about your options under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. ## Not your account at all? Freeze your credit too If something on your report was opened by someone else, a dispute fixes the record, but a credit freeze stops it happening again. A freeze blocks new credit being opened in your name. In the US it is free, and you set it up at each bureau separately. - Have ready: your full name, date of birth, Social Security number and recent addresses. - Freeze at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion on the same day, online or by phone, and save each confirmation and any PIN. - Freeze at Innovis too. It is a fourth bureau that many people forget. - Keep all the confirmations and logins in one safe place you can find months later. - When you apply for credit, a loan or a new rental, ask which bureau will be checked, and lift the freeze at that bureau only, for a set number of days. - Check once a year that the freezes are still in place. A freeze does not affect your credit score, and you can still check your own reports while it is on. Freezes are a US system. In the UK, the closest step is Cifas Protective Registration, which flags applications in your name for extra checks. ## How disputes work in the UK, Canada, and Australia The steps above follow US law. The basic idea is the same elsewhere, but the names, deadlines, and referees differ. ### United Kingdom The three agencies are Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion. Raise the error with the agency that shows it and with the lender that supplied the data. Agencies generally have 28 days to look into a dispute. You can also add a notice of correction, a short explanation in your own words that lenders will see. If a complaint stalls, you can take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service. ### Canada Canada has two bureaus, Equifax Canada and TransUnion Canada, and disputing is free. File with each bureau that shows the error, using its update form, and contact the lender too. If the bureau still will not change the entry, you can add a free consumer statement to your file explaining your side, and raise it with your provincial or territorial consumer affairs office. ### Australia Australia's reporting bodies include Equifax, Experian, and illion, and corrections are free under the Privacy Act. The OAIC advises asking the credit provider first, though you can go straight to a reporting body instead. Either way, they must consult each other to get your request completed. If they agree the information is wrong, they must correct it within 30 days, or a longer period you agree to, and confirm it in writing. If they refuse, they must explain why in writing, and you can complain to the OAIC or use an external dispute resolution scheme such as the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. You can also request a free report from each reporting body every three months to check the fix landed. ## Frequently asked questions ### Does disputing an error hurt my credit score? No. Filing a dispute does not lower your score, and it costs nothing. Only the result can change your score, and removing a false late payment or wrong balance usually helps. If high balances are the real issue, [how to pay off credit card debt fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/) is the more useful read. ### How long does the whole thing take? In the US, plan on about 30 days for the investigation, sometimes up to 45. Add a few days of mailing time at each end if you dispute by post. ### Do I need to dispute with all three bureaus? Only with the bureaus whose reports show the error. Do check all three first, because the same mistake can appear on more than one. ### Is it better to dispute online or by mail? Online is faster to submit. Mail, sent certified with a return receipt, gives dated proof of when the bureau received your dispute, and that date starts the investigation clock. Either way, keep copies of everything. ### Can I dispute something that is true but makes me look bad? No. Disputes are for information that is wrong, incomplete, out of date, or not yours. Accurate negative information is allowed to stay, usually for seven years, and ten years for bankruptcy. Disclaimer: This article is general information about how credit report disputes work, not legal or financial advice for your specific situation. Rules change and differ by country and, in the US and Canada, by state or province. For current guidance, check the CFPB or FTC in the US, or your local regulator. For identity theft, a court case, or a large amount of money, talk to a qualified professional. ## Sources - [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), "How do I dispute an error on my credit report?"](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/how-do-i-dispute-an-error-on-my-credit-report-en-314/) - [Federal Trade Commission (FTC), "Disputing Errors on Your Credit Reports"](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/disputing-errors-your-credit-reports) - [Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC), "Correct your credit report"](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/your-privacy-rights/credit-reporting/correct-your-credit-report)
